subject: Svenska 2
title: Periods in literary history
sourceSummary: Antiquity, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, Romanticism, Realism and Modernism — the characteristics and central authors and works of each period.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the oldest surviving literary works from antiquity still read today?
questions.opener: Think Greek heroic poem, not Roman or medieval.
questions.explanation: The Iliad by Homer was written around the 8th century BC and is counted as one of the oldest surviving literary works still read today. Faust and The Decameron belong to considerably later periods.

questions.prompt: What are the Eufemiavisor ("Songs of Euphemia")?
questions.opener: The name comes from a Norwegian queen who commissioned the works.
choices: Three French chivalric romances translated into Swedish verse in the 14th century
A collection of folk songs from the 17th century
questions.explanation: The Eufemiavisor are three French/German chivalric romances that were translated into Swedish verse on the orders of Queen Euphemia in the early 14th century — important early examples of Swedish fiction. Sweden's first printed book came much later, in the 1480s.

questions.prompt: What characterises the literary ideals of the Renaissance?
questions.opener: The word renaissance means rebirth — of what?
choices: Focus on God and the divine above humankind
Feeling and nature placed above reason
The social problems of everyday life depicted scientifically
Humankind and the ideals of antiquity placed at the centre (humanism)
questions.explanation: The Renaissance (c. 1400–1600) revived antiquity's view of humankind — humanism and earthly life are placed at the centre, in contrast to the God-centred worldview of the Middle Ages. The primacy of feeling and nature belongs instead to Romanticism.

questions.prompt: Which Swedish scientist and author is particularly associated with the Enlightenment's faith in reason and systematisation?
questions.opener: Who systematised nature using reason as a tool?
questions.explanation: Carl von Linné (Linnaeus) represents the Enlightenment's faith in reason, science and systematisation. Bellman wrote in a more sentimental, rococo-inspired style, and Tegnér and Strindberg belong to later periods.

questions.prompt: What was central to Romantic literature, in contrast to the Enlightenment's faith in reason?
questions.opener: What did the Romantics set against the Enlightenment's reason?
choices: The short, compressed expression without figurative language
Feeling, nature, imagination and the past
questions.explanation: Romanticism (c. 1800–1850) foregrounded feeling, nature, the national, and often the medieval past, as a counterweight to the Enlightenment's rationalism. Scientific objectivity and social criticism are instead characteristic of Realism.

questions.prompt: What characterises the realist literature that emerged during the second half of the 19th century?
questions.opener: Think of early Ibsen and Strindberg — what did they want to expose?
choices: A true-to-life depiction of society, often with social criticism
Focus on dreams and the subconscious
questions.explanation: Realism sought to depict reality as it was, often with a critical eye on social problems such as the status of women. Idealisation and fairy-tale worlds belong instead to Romanticism, and free verse without metre is typical of Modernism.

questions.prompt: Explain what is new and different about Modernism's way of writing compared with earlier periods, taking as a starting point, for example, Edith Södergran's poetry.
questions.opener: Think about form, not just content.
questions.answer: Modernism breaks with traditional metres and a unified narrative voice — the text can be fragmentary, use free verse, and depict a fractured inner self, often as a reaction to the upheavals of modern society and the First World War.
steps: Modernism emerges around the turn of the 20th century and gathers pace after the First World War, which shook confidence in progress and reason.
The form changes radically: free verse replaces traditional metres, and the language can be fragmentary or elliptical.
The narration becomes more subjective — interior monologue and fractured perspectives mirror an uncertain, complex reality.
Edith Södergran and, later, the Swedish poets of the 1940s are examples of how Modernism sought new means of expression for a new age.

questions.prompt: Give a quick overview of the literary periods from antiquity to Modernism: time period and characteristics.
questions.answer: Antiquity (c. 800 BC–500 AD): Greco-Roman ideals, epic and drama · The Middle Ages (5th–14th century): religious texts, chivalric romances (e.g. the Eufemiavisor) · The Renaissance (15th–16th century): humankind and antiquity at the centre, humanism · The Enlightenment (18th century): reason, science, criticism of authorities (e.g. Linnaeus) · Romanticism (c. 1800–1850): feeling, nature, the national and the past · Realism/Naturalism (second half of the 19th century): true-to-life depictions of society and social criticism (e.g. Ibsen) · Modernism (from c. 1900): broken forms, free verse, a fractured self (e.g. Södergran).

questions.prompt: Which Roman poet wrote the epic the Aeneid?
questions.opener: The work tells of Aeneas's flight from Troy and the founding of Rome.
questions.explanation: Virgil wrote the Aeneid in the final decades before the Common Era, one of the foremost epics of Roman literature. Homer instead wrote the Greek epics the Iliad and the Odyssey several hundred years earlier, and Ovid is best known for Metamorphoses.

questions.prompt: Which genre was especially common in medieval literature, alongside religious texts?
questions.opener: Think knights, courtly love and adventure.
questions.explanation: Chivalric romances, such as the Eufemiavisor, were a central and popular genre during the Middle Ages alongside religious texts. Science fiction and daily newspapers belong to much later periods.

questions.prompt: Which English playwright, active during the Renaissance, wrote plays such as Hamlet and Macbeth?
questions.opener: One of world literature's most famous playwrights, active around the year 1600.
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare wrote his most famous plays, including Hamlet and Macbeth, around the turn of the 17th century during the English Renaissance. Dickens and Austen instead belong to the 19th century.

questions.prompt: Which work by the French Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire is especially known for its satire of blind optimism and injustice?
questions.opener: The protagonist meets a series of disasters despite his tutor's conviction that everything is for the best.
questions.explanation: Candide (1759) by Voltaire is a satirical tale that mocks philosophical optimism and depicts a series of injustices and disasters. Faust is instead by Goethe, and The Decameron and The Divine Comedy belong to earlier periods.

questions.prompt: Which Swedish author is associated with National Romantic poetry and the work Frithiof's Saga?
questions.opener: The work is based on an Old Norse legend and became very popular during the 19th century.
questions.explanation: Esaias Tegnér wrote Frithiof's Saga, one of the best-known works of Swedish National Romanticism. Strindberg belongs to a later period, Linnaeus to the Enlightenment, and Selma Lagerlöf was active even later.

questions.prompt: Which Norwegian playwright wrote plays such as A Doll's House, which critically examined women's position in society?
questions.opener: This playwright is counted as one of the founders of Realism and of modern drama.
questions.explanation: Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll's House (1879), which critically examined women's role in bourgeois society and became a central work of Realism. Bellman wrote during an entirely different period, and Södergran belongs to Modernism.

questions.prompt: Which poetry collection by Edith Södergran is regarded as a groundbreaking work within Swedish-language Modernism?
questions.opener: The collection was published in 1916 and shocked many readers with its free form.
questions.explanation: Edith Södergran's debut collection Dikter (1916) is regarded as one of the first and most groundbreaking works within Swedish-language Modernism, with its free verse and fractured self. Frithiof's Saga and The Tales of Ensign Stål instead belong to Romanticism.
